title: ID-JAG Runner: the lab's flow, step by step
lede: One PingFederate plays two authorization servers; the MCP server is the resource.

as2.label: Authorization server 2 · PingFederate as resource AS

steps.title: Sign in at authorization server 1 (PingFederate as IdP)
steps.what: The app sends demouser's password grant to PingFederate's token endpoint. AS 1 validates the credentials and issues the access token, refresh token and — on the refresh grant — the ID token.
steps.why: Everything downstream starts from tokens AS 1 issued.

steps.title: Authorization server 1 mints the ID-JAG
steps.what: The app exchanges its ID token (or refresh or access token) at the same PingFederate, now in its enterprise-issuer role. It validates the subject token, applies the idjagpolicy checks, and signs an ID-JAG — a short-lived grant naming the user, this app, and the target resource server.
steps.why: The ID-JAG is a signed pass from AS 1: no second login, and the IdP stays in control of who may reach what.

steps.title: Authorization server 2 redeems the ID-JAG
steps.what: The app hands the ID-JAG to the second authorization server — the resource AS role — as a jwt-bearer assertion. AS 2 downloads AS 1's JWKS, checks the signature, issuer, audience and expiry, and issues its own access token for the MCP resource.
steps.why: No password, no consent screen: trust flows from the signature, and AS 2 issues a token for its own resource.

steps.title: The MCP server would receive the call
steps.what: The app would call the MCP server with the access token AS 2 issued. In this lab introspection stands in for the API: it shows exactly what the MCP server would learn from the token (active, sub, scope, client_id).
steps.why: The MCP server trusts only tokens AS 2 issued — the same token type a real gateway or API would enforce.
